content: Palliative care, including pediatric palliative care (PPC), plays a critical role in healthcare systems. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), serious or life-threatening health conditions are often diagnosed at secondary or tertiary hospitals, where palliative care and symptom management are typically initiated. When patients do not require or cannot access care at higher-level hospitals, and their symptoms are not complex or resistant to treatment, palliative care can be initiated at first-level hospitals. Home care plans should be established, and follow-up care can be provided by community health centers (CHCs) or community health workers (CHWs). In rare cases of severe, refractory suffering, such as non-viable premature neonates with respiratory failure or patients with end-stage cancer experiencing severe pain, inpatient end-of-life care may be necessary at any level of the healthcare system. If families are unable to provide adequate care at home, CHCs should offer inpatient end-of-life care for a limited number of patients. However, most patients should be able to remain at home with follow-up care provided by CHWs, CHCs, or outpatient palliative care clinics. National healthcare policies must clearly define the types of palliative care services required at each level of the healthcare system and specify the training needed for providers at each level. Palliative care interventions can be delivered through various platforms, including mobile outreach, home care, CHCs, and hospitals. For patients with well-controlled symptoms, CHWs can provide regular surveillance and emotional support, while nurses, doctors, or social workers with basic palliative care training can offer outpatient care and home visits as needed. In some cases, inpatient hospice care may be required if families cannot provide care at home. At higher-level hospitals, small palliative care teams, including part-time doctors with basic or intermediate training, can provide outpatient and inpatient care. Ideally, major cancer centers and general hospitals should have palliative care teams led by specialist physicians. These teams should manage inpatient palliative care wards and outpatient clinics, ensuring comprehensive care for patients with complex needs. Effective communication between providers at all levels of the healthcare system is crucial. For example, CHWs must be able to quickly contact nurses or supervisors at CHCs, and providers at CHCs must have access to district-level supervisors for advice on complicated cases. Similarly, third-level hospital providers must communicate with CHCs to coordinate home-based palliative care. Mobile phones are typically used for this communication, as texting is often inadequate for conveying critical clinical information. In LMICs with underdeveloped referral systems, standardized palliative care handover forms should be used to document patients' clinical and social histories, treatments, and care goals. Budgets for palliative care should include funding for telecommunications, printing of forms, and transportation for CHC staff to visit patients at home. Palliative care training must be integrated into healthcare education systems at all levels. Basic training should be included in undergraduate medical and nursing curricula and in-service training for primary care providers. Intermediate training should be offered to healthcare workers who routinely manage patients with life-threatening illnesses, such as those in oncology, pediatrics, geriatrics, and internal medicine. Specialist training programs should prepare healthcare professionals to manage complex palliative care needs and should last at least one year, depending on national regulations. In LMICs, efforts should focus on developing palliative care specialist training programs to meet the needs of their populations. Generalist clinicians, such as family doctors and primary care nurses, should be trained to provide pediatric palliative care (PPC) when pediatric specialists are unavailable. Training should emphasize essential competencies, including symptom management, communication, care planning, and professional resilience. Generalists providing PPC should have access to advice from pediatricians or palliative care specialists as needed, particularly in rural areas. Palliative care education should include both classroom and bedside teaching. Basic training should cover approximately 35 hours and may be integrated into existing courses or offered as a standalone course. Intermediate training, lasting about 70 hours, should be included in specialist training curricula for fields that manage serious illnesses. Specialist training programs should prepare clinicians to provide direct palliative care and lead hospital-based palliative care teams. Access to essential medicines, such as strong opioids like morphine, is critical for managing pain in patients with cancer, HIV/AIDS, and other serious illnesses. Despite being included on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, morphine remains inaccessible to 75% of the global population. This lack of access leaves millions of terminal cancer and end-stage HIV/AIDS patients suffering from untreated pain each year.
